idiom_name: Django's built-in Permission/Group model (user.has_perm, @permission_required, Group as role) plus DRF permission classes; Oso/pycasbin where the policy is code or a table
implementation_notes: Django ships RBAC in contrib.auth: every model gets add/change/delete/view Permission rows, a Group is a role, and assigning a user to a group grants the group's permissions - user.has_perm('shop.pause_transfers') and @permission_required('shop.pause_transfers') are the decision primitives, with django-guardian adding per-object permissions. In a DRF API the same decision appears as a permission class (see authorization-enforcer): a HasRole/HasPermission class implementing has_permission (and has_object_permission for the owning-object case) listed in permission_classes, which must be deny-by-default because DRF's global default is AllowAny. When permissions are better held as data than as rows, pycasbin gives the same Enforce(sub, obj, act) table model as the other Casbin ports, and Oso keeps the rule in a Polar policy - a resource block mapping roles to permissions and a has_role rule reading your data store. Assign roles, not permissions: grant through Group (or a role table), never per user, so the matrix stays reviewable.
pitfalls: DRF's DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES is AllowAny; a view that forgets permission_classes is open - set a deny-by-default global default.
Granting a permission straight to a user (user.user_permissions.add) instead of to a group recreates the unreviewable per-user matrix RBAC exists to avoid.
Django's ModelBackend unions user and group permissions per check, so caching get_all_permissions() across a role change serves stale rights; invalidate on assignment.
Object-level checks (has_object_permission, guardian) are skipped for list endpoints and on create; scope the queryset and check creation separately.
Reading roles from request.data or a client-supplied claim lets the caller escalate; resolve membership from request.user server-side.
